analysis.one_liner: Forces federal agencies to quickly agree with states on cleaning PFAS contamination from federal facilities.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 10 Senate cosponsors including 3 Republicans, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on May 8, 2019 and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets PFAS — 'forever chemicals' linked to health problems — that leak from federal sites, especially military bases, into drinking water and soil. When a state's governor asks, federal agencies would have to move quickly to sign cleanup agreements with the state, and those agreements must meet the toughest applicable water standard. If an agency drags its feet for a year, the President would have to explain the delay to Congress and the affected communities' representatives.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents near contaminated federal facilities — particularly communities around military bases like those in Michigan, where firefighting foam tainted drinking water — get a faster, firmer path to cleanup and safer water.

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal agencies, on a state's request, to work expeditiously to finalize cooperative agreements for testing, monitoring, removal, and remedial actions addressing PFAS contamination from federal facilities.
Requires cleanup agreements to meet or exceed the most stringent applicable standard — state drinking water standards, federal health advisories, or limits under federal environmental laws.
If no agreement is finalized within a year, the President must report to Congress and affected-state lawmakers explaining the delay and giving a timeline.
Allows federal agencies to contract directly with local water utilities and state, local, or tribal governments to address contaminated water.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies — chiefly the Department of Defense — would bear the cost of cleanup and testing at their facilities, and the federal government covers remediation that would otherwise fall on state and local water systems.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal government, mainly the Defense Department

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on deadlines and reports rather than hard enforcement: if agencies still fail to finalize agreements, the consequence is a written explanation to Congress, not automatic action.
It addresses contamination from federal facilities only, so PFAS pollution from industrial and commercial sources is left to other laws.
Accelerating cleanup could divert existing federal environmental and defense funds, and Deferral of DoD liability disputes with states is not fully resolved by cooperative agreements alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities living with PFAS-tainted water, the benefits — faster cleanup agreements, the strictest standards applying, and public accounting for delays — clearly outweigh the administrative costs to federal agencies. The bill's main weakness is that it leans on reporting rather than penalties, so an uncooperative agency could still stall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in May 2019, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Stabenow introduced the bill on May 8, 2019 with 10 cosponsors, 7 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action was recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies — particularly the Defense Department — avoided new obligations to fast-track cleanup agreements with states, and the bill's accountability reporting requirement never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PFAS Accountability Act of 2019 on May 8, 2019.

for.name: 10 of 100 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: 7 Democrats (Carper, Shaheen, Peters, Hassan, Baldwin, Cantwell, Manchin) and 3 Republicans (Rubio, Tillis, Burr).

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2019 and never reported it out or held a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: 7 of 11 senators backing the bill were Democrats and 3 were Republicans, though no committee or floor vote ever tested the support.

industries.note: Military bases are a major source of PFAS contamination from firefighting foam; the bill would have obligated DoD to expedite cleanup agreements with states and meet the strictest standards. Its death left federal facilities free of this added accountability.

industries.industry: Water utilities (public water systems and treatment works)
industries.note: The bill would let local water utilities contract directly with federal agencies to address contaminated water, easing the financial burden of PFAS cleanup on ratepayers.
